In 1896, American inventor Jesse Reno installed what he called an "inclined ________" at Coney Island in New York — a continuously moving conveyor belt set at an angle of about 25 degrees that carried passengers upward while they stood or crouched on grooved wooden slats. It was more of a novelty ride than a practical device, carrying around 75,000 passengers in its first two weeks. Separately, inventor Charles Seeberger developed a true ____-based moving _________ and brought his design to company X in 1899. X acquired Seeberger's design, refined it by combining it with elements of Reno's approach, and debuted a working prototype at the Paris Exposition of 1900, where it won first prize. X coined the name Y for the device, combining a  Latin word with the suffix of another X invention that had already transformed urban life. The word Y is now used in virtually every language on earth, often borrowed directly from English. ID X (5 points) and Y (5 points).
